title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    category: registry_event

falsepositives:

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003

logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

            - '\brave.exe'

level: high

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'

Popular WordPress Plugin Scripts Tampered to Plant Hidden Backdoors on Sites

The Hacker News
2026-06-15 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An attacker tampered with trusted JavaScript files used by WordPress sites running PushEngage, OptinMonster, and TrustPulse, turning those files into a way to break into the sites. When a site administrator was logged in as the file loaded, the code created an admin account under the attacker's control and installed a hidden plugin that opened a way back in. Ordinary visitors did not trigger it

Egress to Awesome Motive backdoor C2 (tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any outbound DNS resolution or TCP connection from internal infrastructure to the Sansec-disclosed lookalike domain tidio[.]cc or the C2 IP 84.201.6.54 (Ultahost AS214036). These are the exfiltration destinations the tampered PushEngage/OptinMonster/TrustPulse JavaScript writes to once it has hijacked a logged-in admin session. Rationale: Sansec disclosure and the PushEngage incident note both confirm tidio[.]cc (lookalike of tidio.com, registered 2026-04-28) and 84.201.6.54 (Ultahost AS214036) as the credential-exfil + C2 endpoints. Either signal in isolation is high-fidelity — they are not legitimate destinations for any tenant. Cross-checked against Sansec's public research page. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/optinmonster-supply-chain-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/popular-wordpress-plugin-scripts.html

  • Security researcher / DFIR analyst manually validating the IOC from a sandbox VM in the corporate network
  • Threat-intel platform ingest fetching the domain for enrichment (Recorded Future / VT pivot)
  • Phishing-simulation vendor unrelated test traffic happening to resolve a same-IP host on AS214036
  • Outbound from a deception/honeypot box intentionally beaconing
  • Backup/forensic image of a compromised tenant being analysed on internal infra
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or isempty(InitiatingProcessFileName) // exclude analyst browser pivots from triage workstations; keep server-side hits
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the originating host. If it's a WordPress / WooCommerce server, treat as confirmed compromise — pull the connection's process tree (or Apache/PHP-FPM access logs around the connection time) to see which PHP file made the request. 2) Contain: block tidio.cc and 84.201.6.54 at egress; isolate the source host from the network; rotate wp-config.php salts, DB credentials, all admin passwords, and any CDN/API keys held on that host. 3) Hunt: filesystem-scan wp-content/plugins for content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer (see UC2), audit wp_users for developer_api1 or dev_* accounts, and review web access logs for /cdn-cgi/* paths to tidio.cc (see UC3). Assume additional persistence — Sansec says removing the named plugin and account may not be enough.
let bad_ips = dynamic(["84.201.6.54"]);
let bad_domains = dynamic(["tidio.cc",".tidio.cc"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP in (bad_ips)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (bad_domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp asc
let bad_ips = dynamic(["84.201.6.54"]);
let bad_domains = dynamic(["tidio.cc"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where DestinationIP in (bad_ips)
     or RequestURL has_any (bad_domains)
     or DestinationHostName has_any (bad_domains)
  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName,
            DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod,
            RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
),
( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where Name has_any (bad_domains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses=Result
),
( ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where DstIpAddr in (bad_ips) or DstHostname has_any (bad_domains) or Url has_any (bad_domains)
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
)
| order by TimeGenerated asc
title: WordPress Plugin Supply Chain C2 - tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54
id: 9a3c2f74-1f25-4a7e-8b6f-43d9d9d3a311
status: experimental
description: Detects outbound connections to the Sansec-disclosed C2 used by the OptinMonster/TrustPulse/PushEngage supply chain backdoor (June 2026).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/popular-wordpress-plugin-scripts.html
  - https://sansec.io/research/optinmonster-supply-chain-attack
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1567
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ip:
    DestinationIp: '84.201.6.54'
  selection_domain:
    DestinationHostname|contains: 'tidio.cc'
  condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
level: high
falsepositives:
  - None expected; tidio.cc is a known-bad lookalike domain and 84.201.6.54 is an attacker-controlled Ultahost IP
(@network.destination.ip:84.201.6.54 OR @DestinationIp:84.201.6.54 OR @network.destination.domain:(tidio.cc OR *.tidio.cc) OR @DestinationHostname:(tidio.cc OR *.tidio.cc) OR @dns.question.name:(tidio.cc OR *.tidio.cc) OR @DomainName:(tidio.cc OR *.tidio.cc) OR @http.url:*tidio.cc* OR @RequestURL:*tidio.cc*) AND source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd OR linux.syslog OR proxy OR firewall)
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)tidio\.cc$/i) OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemoteAddressIP4="84.201.6.54")) OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6 RemoteAddressIP6=*)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=[count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp)])
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcaddr, dstaddr, dstport, protocol, action, bytes
| filter dstaddr = "84.201.6.54"
| stats count(*) as flows, sum(bytes) as bytes_out by srcaddr, dstaddr, dstport, action
| sort flows desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.dest="84.201.6.54" OR Web.url="*tidio.cc*" OR Web.dest="tidio.cc") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | append [ | tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_port values(All_Traffic.app) as app from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="84.201.6.54" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="tidio.cc" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*.tidio.cc") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` ] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as url values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.dest="84.201.6.54" OR Web.url="*tidio.cc*" OR Web.dest="tidio.cc") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | append [ | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_port values(All_Traffic.app) as app from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="84.201.6.54" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="tidio.cc" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*.tidio.cc") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` ] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Rogue WordPress backdoor plugin folder created (content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer) AIInstallation High
Hunts for the on-disk artefacts of the Sansec-disclosed hidden plugin that the tampered Awesome Motive JavaScript installs once it has hijacked an admin session. The plugin folders are content-delivery-helper ("Content Delivery Helper") and database-optimizer ("Database Optimizer"); both names are chosen to look like routine performance plugins. Rationale: Sansec's IOC matrix explicitly names content-delivery-helper and database-optimizer as the two backdoor plugin folder names dropped by the tampered Awesome Motive JS. Neither name corresponds to a real Awesome Motive product — any file create under wp-content/plugins/<either name>/ is essentially a binary IOC. Cross-checked against Sansec research page. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/optinmonster-supply-chain-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/popular-wordpress-plugin-scripts.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1505 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-hunting team intentionally deploying the IOC names in a lab to test detection
  • Backup/restore process re-creating the path from a compromised image being analysed
  • Security tool unpacking a malware sample into a path that happens to include the folder name
  • DFIR consultant copying evidence onto a forensic file share with the same path
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a production WordPress server and pull `ls -la wp-content/plugins/{content-delivery-helper,database-optimizer}` plus the PHP files inside — these are the web shell. Capture file mtimes and inode metadata before touching them. 2) Contain: isolate the web server, do NOT just `rm -rf` the folder (preserve for IR); rotate wp-config.php SALT/AUTH_KEY values, DB creds, admin passwords, and all stored API keys (CDN, SMTP, payment). Take the site offline behind maintenance mode. 3) Hunt: enumerate wp_users for developer_api1 / dev_* accounts and any user with administrator role created since 2026-06-12; grep web access logs for outbound traffic to tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54 (UC1); scan the entire docroot for newly-created PHP files mtime>=2026-06-12. Assume additional backdoors per Sansec guidance.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/wp-content/plugins/content-delivery-helper",
                            "/wp-content/plugins/database-optimizer",
                            @"\wp-content\plugins\content-delivery-helper",
                            @"\wp-content\plugins\database-optimizer")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp asc
union isfuzzy=true
( ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
  | where TargetFilePath has_any ("/wp-content/plugins/content-delivery-helper",
                                  "/wp-content/plugins/database-optimizer")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
            ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
),
( Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where Facility in ("auth","kern","daemon","user")
  | where SyslogMessage has_any ("wp-content/plugins/content-delivery-helper",
                                  "wp-content/plugins/database-optimizer")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
)
| order by TimeGenerated asc
title: WordPress Backdoor Plugin Folder Created (content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer)
id: 4b1ee8c2-3afd-4d2b-9c7d-7c0d3b6d2c1e
status: experimental
description: Detects file creation under wp-content/plugins for the two backdoor plugin folder names disclosed by Sansec in the June 2026 Awesome Motive supply-chain attack.
references:

Web access to backdoor /cdn-cgi/ paths on tidio.cc lookalike domain AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Cloudflare-mimicking /cdn-cgi/ URI path on the lookalike tidio[.]cc domain that the tampered Awesome Motive JS POSTs new admin credentials and site fingerprint to. The path mimics legitimate Cloudflare worker URLs to blend in with proxy log noise. Targets proxy / WAF / web access logs. Rationale: The PushEngage incident note and Sansec disclosure both call out tidio[.]cc/cdn-cgi/ paths as the exfil channel — the /cdn-cgi/ prefix mimics Cloudflare to evade casual proxy-log review. The combination of tidio.cc host + /cdn-cgi/ path is article-specific and high-confidence; pairing with the 84.201.6.54 IP makes this near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/optinmonster-supply-chain-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/popular-wordpress-plugin-scripts.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1567.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst pivoting on the IOC from a triage workstation through the corporate proxy
  • Internal threat-intel enrichment hitting the URL to fetch the page contents
  • Security scanner (URLscan/Joe Sandbox proxy) crawling the domain
  • Backup of a compromised customer site replayed through internal egress for forensic review
  • User on a compromised personal device VPN'd into corp accidentally triggering the JS
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "VirusTotalApiClient" and RequestClientApplication !has "urlscan" // suppress threat-intel pivots
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source — if it is a WordPress / e-commerce server, treat as confirmed compromise; if it is a workstation, check whether the user is a WP admin on any tenant we manage and whether their browser session was used during the June 12-14 window. Pull the full proxy request including POST body if captured. 2) Contain: blackhole tidio.cc + 84.201.6.54 at the proxy/firewall; isolate the source; if a WP admin's browser triggered this, force a session revoke on every WordPress site they administrate and rotate their site admin credentials + WP salts. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP/host across the last 30 days for any tidio.cc DNS or 84.201.6.54 TCP (UC1); enumerate which Awesome Motive plugins were active on the customer sites the admin manages; check those sites' wp-content/plugins for content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer (UC2).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (RemoteUrl has "tidio.cc" and RemoteUrl has "/cdn-cgi/")
     or (RemoteIP == "84.201.6.54")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp asc
let bad_host = "tidio.cc";
let bad_ip = "84.201.6.54";
union isfuzzy=true
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where (DestinationHostName =~ bad_host and RequestURL has "/cdn-cgi/")
       or (RequestURL has strcat(bad_host,"/cdn-cgi/"))
       or DestinationIP == bad_ip
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName,
            RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, DeviceAction
),
( W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where csUriStem has "/cdn-cgi/" and (csReferer has bad_host or csUriQuery has bad_host)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csReferer, csUserAgent, scStatus
),
( ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where (Url has bad_host and Url has "/cdn-cgi/") or DstIpAddr == bad_ip
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpResponseBodyBytes
)
| order by TimeGenerated asc
source:(proxy OR firewall OR windows.sysmon OR linux.syslog) AND ((@http.url:*tidio.cc/cdn-cgi/* OR @http.url:*tidio.cc%2Fcdn-cgi%2F*) OR (@network.destination.domain:tidio.cc AND @http.url_details.path:*/cdn-cgi/*) OR (@RequestURL:*tidio.cc/cdn-cgi/*) OR @network.destination.ip:84.201.6.54)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)tidio\.cc$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="84.201.6.54" OR cidr("84.201.6.54/32", field=RemoteAddressIP4)}, field=aid, include=[ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=[count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp)])
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.user_agent) as user_agent values(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*tidio.cc/cdn-cgi/*" OR (Web.dest="tidio.cc" AND Web.url="*/cdn-cgi/*") OR Web.dest="84.201.6.54") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | where http_method="POST" OR bytes_out>500
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.user_agent) as user_agent values(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*tidio.cc/cdn-cgi/*" OR (Web.dest="tidio.cc" AND Web.url="*/cdn-cgi/*") OR Web.dest="84.201.6.54") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | where http_method="POST" OR bytes_out>500
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003

logsource:
    category: file_access

detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'

        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

            - '\firefox.exe'

    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10795")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10795")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access

    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3d371ef71e40c34a75c168d464d47db096f386499d9aa88d4e16b63cd4acda25") or SHA1 in~ ("3d371ef71e40c34a75c168d464d47db096f386499d9aa88d4e16b63cd4acda25") or MD5 in~ ("3d371ef71e40c34a75c168d464d47db096f386499d9aa88d4e16b63cd4acda25")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3d371ef71e40c34a75c168d464d47db096f386499d9aa88d4e16b63cd4acda25") or SHA1 in~ ("3d371ef71e40c34a75c168d464d47db096f386499d9aa88d4e16b63cd4acda25") or MD5 in~ ("3d371ef71e40c34a75c168d464d47db096f386499d9aa88d4e16b63cd4acda25")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["3d371ef71e40c34a75c168d464d47db096f386499d9aa88d4e16b63cd4acda25"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)

                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Palo Alto Warns of Active Exploitation of PAN-OS GlobalProtect VPN Flaw

The Hacker NewsCyber Security News
2026-06-15 7 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Palo Alto Networks has revealed that it has observed "active exploitation" of a recently disclosed PAN-OS vulnerability by an unknown threat actor to obtain unauthorized access to GlobalProtect portals. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-0257 (CVSS score: 7.8), an authentication bypass flaw affecting the portal and gateway components of PAN-OS software that could be exploited by bad

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] PAN-OS GlobalProtect connection from CVE-2026-0257 exploit source IPs
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PAN-OS GlobalProtect connection with CVE-2026-0257 PoC default client fingerprint
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
PAN-OS GlobalProtect connection from CVE-2026-0257 exploit source IPs AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound connections to the GlobalProtect portal/gateway from the nine attacker IPs Palo Alto published as confirmed exploit infrastructure for CVE-2026-0257. Pivots are the PAN firewall traffic / GP gateway logs and (as a side channel) any internal host that ever reached out to the same IPs. Rationale: Uses the exact nine source IPs Palo Alto Networks published for the CVE-2026-0257 active-exploitation campaign — these are not generic VPN scanners but confirmed exploit infrastructure. Cross-checked against the CISA KEV listing for the CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://security.paloaltonetworks.com/CVE-2026-0257
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IP rotation by a benign cloud provider re-assigning one of the IOC IPs to a legitimate customer after the campaign ends
  • SOC red-team exercise simulating the PoC from a known IP that overlaps the IOC list
  • Threat-intel vendor scanner replaying the IOC list against the GP portal for validation
  • Outbound proxy / tunnel reassigned the IOC IP to an unrelated tenant
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("redteam-test","vuln-scanner-svc") and not (DestinationIP startswith "10." and Activity has "test")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the full GP session record — does endpoint_os_version match the PoC fingerprint and is source_user_info.domain empty? Identify whether the gateway-connected event resulted in an actual VPN tunnel (Palo Alto's blog flagged that only a fraction of probed devices established sessions). Step 2 (contain): block the offending source IP on the perimeter and the GP portal ACL; if a tunnel was established, force-disconnect the GP session and revoke the assigned IP pool address. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the assigned internal tunnel IP across DHCP/firewall logs for any east-west movement, query AD for authentications attributing to the GP-assigned source, and confirm CVE-2026-0257 patch level on the affected appliance.

PAN-OS GlobalProtect connection with CVE-2026-0257 PoC default client fingerprint AIExploitation High
Hunts for the hardcoded client configuration values from the public CVE-2026-0257 PoC exploit: endpoint_os_version of 'Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit' combined with an empty source_user_info.domain on a gateway-connected event. Palo Alto explicitly tells customers to search for this fingerprint. Rationale: Uses the two hardcoded client-configuration strings Palo Alto Networks explicitly told customers to search for in GlobalProtect logs (endpoint_os_version='Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit' and empty source_user_info.domain). These are PoC defaults that no legitimate enterprise Windows 10 client emits together at scale. Cross-checked with the Palo Alto CVE-2026-0257 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://security.paloaltonetworks.com/CVE-2026-0257 • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A BYOD Windows 10 Pro user joining the VPN from a non-AD-joined personal laptop where the GP client did not populate the domain field
  • Newly-imaged Windows 10 Pro lab/test endpoint connected before AD-join completed
  • Contractor / guest GP access tier that does not require domain membership and ships Windows 10 Pro hosts
  • Internal red-team running the public PoC during an authorised exercise
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<known-byod-egress-cidr>") and DestinationHostName !has "guest-gp" and SourceUserName !in~ ("redteam-test","contractor-pool")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the matched session — does the assigned tunnel IP map to a known asset, and was the gateway-connected event followed by any authenticated user activity on the tunnel? Cross-check the source IP against the IOC list from UC1 to confirm if it's the same campaign. Step 2 (contain): force-disconnect the GP session, block the source IP on the portal, and verify the PAN-OS appliance is patched against CVE-2026-0257. Step 3 (hunt): query the past 30 days of GP logs for the same fingerprint across all gateways, enumerate which internal subnets/resources the tunnel IP touched, and review any subsequent AD authentications originating from the assigned tunnel IP pool.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Palo Alto Networks"
| where DeviceProduct has "GlobalProtect" or Message has "globalprotect"
| where Activity has "gateway-connected" or Message has "gateway-connected" or DeviceEventClassID has "globalprotect"
| where Message has "Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit"
| where isempty(SourceUserName) or SourceUserName == "" or SourceUserName == "-" or Message has "domain=\"\"" or Message has "source_user_info.domain="
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DeviceCustomString1, DeviceCustomString2, DeviceCustomString3, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0257")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0257")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7b03fb383a5ce784a3cb9b0f8a76a84e984d14e553de5d98faff3d07d9793085") or SHA1 in~ ("7b03fb383a5ce784a3cb9b0f8a76a84e984d14e553de5d98faff3d07d9793085") or MD5 in~ ("7b03fb383a5ce784a3cb9b0f8a76a84e984d14e553de5d98faff3d07d9793085")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7b03fb383a5ce784a3cb9b0f8a76a84e984d14e553de5d98faff3d07d9793085") or SHA1 in~ ("7b03fb383a5ce784a3cb9b0f8a76a84e984d14e553de5d98faff3d07d9793085") or MD5 in~ ("7b03fb383a5ce784a3cb9b0f8a76a84e984d14e553de5d98faff3d07d9793085")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["7b03fb383a5ce784a3cb9b0f8a76a84e984d14e553de5d98faff3d07d9793085"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Sniper Dz Scams Target MENA Users via Fake Facebook Offers and Browser Alerts

The Hacker News
2026-06-15 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of fraudulent activity targeting users across the Middle East and North Africa by employing various fraudulent Facebook accounts impersonating politicians, public figures, and trusted organizations. "These accounts promoted fake offers, including free mobile internet packages, financial compensation, and government subsidy programs," Group-IB

ATT&CKT1190 T1555.003 T1566
Domainswin.feezossl.xyz win.anababayala.com aff.bnaosf1he.shop offer.raviral.com raviral.com sniperdz.com automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Sniper Dz PhaaS infrastructure delivered via inbound email URLs · [LLM] User click-through on Sniper Dz redirect URL (Safe Links) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS or network egress to Sniper Dz infrastructure (IP and host indicators) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Sniper Dz PhaaS infrastructure delivered via inbound email URLs AIDelivery High
Inbound message contains a URL pointing to known Sniper Dz redirector or landing-page infrastructure (sniperdz.com, raviral.com, win.feezossl.xyz, etc.). Hunts the delivery vector even when the lure was originally posted on Facebook and forwarded to the victim via mail share. Group-IB tied these domains to the post-INTERPOL-takedown resurgence of the kit. Rationale: Uses the specific IOC domains the article enumerates as Sniper Dz infrastructure. Inbound + URL-domain match on a curated list is high-fidelity because these are not generic services; the only FP risk is a security analyst forwarding the IOC list internally.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst forwarding the IOC list or Group-IB write-up via email
  • Threat-intel digest emails that quote the URLs verbatim (Recorded Future, Group-IB newsletter)
  • Phishing-simulation vendor URLs that intentionally mimic these domains for awareness training
  • User reporting the phishing email back through a Report Phish add-in (causes the same URL to traverse the wire again)
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromAddress !endswith "@yourorg.com" and RecipientEmailAddress !in~ ("soc@yourorg.com","phishing-reports@yourorg.com","abuse@yourorg.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the full recipient list for the matching NetworkMessageId via EmailEvents and check whether any of them subsequently appear in UrlClickEvents for the same NetworkMessageId — that escalates this from delivery to click-through. Step 2 (contain): soft-delete or quarantine outstanding copies via Defender Threat Explorer for the NetworkMessageId, and add the matched UrlDomain values to the tenant block list. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsEvents on the same domains for the last 14 days across the recipient population to find anyone who opened the URL outside Safe Links (clicked from mobile, copy-pasted into another browser).
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | extend HostLower = tolower(UrlDomain)
    | where HostLower has_any (SniperDzDomains) or Url has_any (SniperDzDomains)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, ReportId
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor in~ ("Proofpoint","Mimecast","Cisco","Microsoft")
| where RequestURL has_any (SniperDzDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (SniperDzDomains) or Message has_any (SniperDzDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, Activity, DeviceAction, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

User click-through on Sniper Dz redirect URL (Safe Links) AIDelivery High
Safe Links UrlClickEvents for one of the Sniper Dz infrastructure domains, including ClickedThrough where the user bypassed the warning. This is the highest-fidelity post-delivery signal in the kill chain and the one that warrants immediate user contact, because the next step in the article's described funnel is browser-notification permission grant and TDS routing. Rationale: UrlClickEvents is the only Defender table that confirms the user actually opened the link (vs. it merely landed in their inbox). IsClickedThrough==true is an extra escalation signal because Safe Links warned them and they proceeded anyway — high-priority user-contact case. Domains are taken verbatim from the article's IOC list. Sentinel has no equivalent table without M365 Defender, so sentinel_kql is intentionally empty.
ATT&CKT1204.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst manually clicking the URL inside Safe Links during triage of UC1
  • Phishing-reporter user clicking the link before reporting (legitimate but operationally noisy)
  • Web-content categorisation services that crawl through Safe Links
  • Sandbox / detonation vendor accounts that follow URLs from quarantined mail
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("soc-analyst@yourorg.com","ir-handler@yourorg.com") and IPAddress !in ("<known-sandbox-egress-ips>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify AccountUpn and pull DeviceInfo to map to device; pull DeviceNetworkEvents on the user's primary device for the 30 min after ClickTime — look for follow-on traffic to the redirect chain or notification-service VAPID endpoints. Step 2 (contain): reset the user's session cookies for the mail tenant and force MFA re-prompt; if the user reports they granted browser-notification permission, push a managed-browser policy that revokes notification grants for the IOC domains. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the matched Url back to EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo on the same NetworkMessageId to identify the original sender and other recipients; check for secondary clicks from the same campaign within 24h across the tenant.
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| extend UrlLower = tolower(Url)
| where UrlLower has_any (SniperDzDomains)
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, Subject, RecipientEmailAddress
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, Workload, SenderFromAddress, Subject
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
UrlClickEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| extend UrlLower = tolower(Url)
| where UrlLower has_any (SniperDzDomains)
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, Subject, RecipientEmailAddress
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, Workload, SenderFromAddress, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
DNS or network egress to Sniper Dz infrastructure (IP and host indicators) AICommand & Control Medium
Direct EDR/DNS observation of a workstation contacting one of the Sniper Dz hosting IPs (65.60.9.236, 108.178.23.118, 184.154.10.254) or attempting to resolve one of the named scam domains. Catches the case where the user reached the link outside Safe Links (mobile mail, SMS lure, Facebook in-app browser) and only the network egress survives. Rationale: Article enumerates three IPs (65.60.9.236, 108.178.23.118, 184.154.10.254) and nine domains as the campaign's hosting / redirect / TDS infrastructure. IP-membership + DNS-query-name match is the cleanest IOC pivot available and survives the scenario where Safe Links never observed the click (mobile, SMS lure, Facebook in-app browser).
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion box pulling the same IOCs from an OSINT source (e.g. abuse.ch fetch)
  • Researcher sandbox detonating the URLs from a corporate egress
  • URL-scanning service (urlscan, VirusTotal) called from an internal pipeline that resolves IOC domains
  • Pantheonsite.io is shared-tenant hosting — false positives possible if dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io is later reassigned to a legitimate customer (revalidate domain ownership quarterly)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("<threat-intel-sandbox-hostnames>") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe") | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-threatintel","svc-urlscan")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the device, the user, and the originating process — if InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser (msedge.exe/chrome.exe/firefox.exe) check UrlClickEvents and EmailEvents for the same user within the prior 30 min to identify the lure source; if it's a non-browser process, treat as elevated severity. Step 2 (contain): block the IPs at perimeter and the domains in the secure web gateway / DNS resolver; revoke browser notification permission via managed policy for affected users. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the user across DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsEvents for related redirect domains (Linktree / Linkbio destinations that ended in the same IPs), and across the wider population for any device that resolved any of the IOC domains in the last 30 days.
let SniperDzIPs = dynamic(["65.60.9.236","108.178.23.118","184.154.10.254"]);
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in (SniperDzIPs)
   or (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and tolower(RemoteUrl) has_any (SniperDzDomains))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let SniperDzIPs = dynamic(["65.60.9.236","108.178.23.118","184.154.10.254"]);
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where tolower(Name) has_any (SniperDzDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Indicator=Name, Source="DnsEvents" ),
( ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where tolower(DnsQuery) has_any (SniperDzDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SrcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=DnsQuery, Source="ImDnsActivity" ),
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DestinationIP in (SniperDzIPs) or tolower(DestinationHostName) has_any (SniperDzDomains) or tolower(RequestURL) has_any (SniperDzDomains)

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

date: 2026/05/02

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'

            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'

            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

GS-Netcat reverse shell beaconing to gs.thc.org relay AICommand & Control High
Hunts Velvet Ant's modified GS-Netcat reverse shell calling out to the hardcoded gs.thc.org relay domain on compromised internet-facing Linux servers. The shell is dropped as a masqueraded system component and provides encrypted remote shell access — DNS/connection to that specific relay is the cleanest article-derived IOC. Rationale: Article names the hardcoded GS-Netcat relay implicitly via the pre-extracted IOC gs.thc.org (gsocket.io public relay). Sygnia's disassembly screenshot (image [3]) confirmed the embedded relay. Single high-fidelity IOC — any host in our environment resolving this is hard to explain benignly. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1047/ • https://github.com/hackerschoice/gsocket
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team engagement using gsocket/gs-netcat for C2 simulation
  • Researcher / pentester home lab connecting personal device to corporate VPN
  • Reverse-engineering training where students download gsocket samples
  • Misconfigured DNS resolver leaking lab traffic to corporate logging
